cases.title: The box that rebuilt world trade

skeleton.brief: Show drastic drop in shipping cost from 1956 to 1966
Explain break bulk cargo handling before containers
Describe 1960s debate over container size and ISO standardization
Explain Vietnam War's role in container shipping adoption
Detail ports relocating to accommodate container infrastructure
Highlight today's massive scale of container movements

narration.text: In 1956, loading a ship cost about five dollars and eighty cents a ton. Within a decade, the same ton cost just sixteen cents.
Before containers, cargo moved as break bulk: sacks, crates, and barrels, each handled by gangs of dockworkers and stacked by eye. Ships could spend longer in port than at sea.

asset_request.description: dockworkers loading break bulk cargo with sacks and crates on a busy port
asset_request.guidance: A clear daylight photo of dockworkers manually loading sacks and crates on a ship, showing the labor-intensive process.

narration.text: The 1960s were spent arguing about container size. Ports, railways, and truckers all wanted different boxes. The standard settled when ISO fixed corner castings and lengths between 1968 and 1970.
Vietnam made container shipping real. The US military needed reliable resupply across the Pacific, and containers were the only way to do it, funding ships and cranes later used in civilian trade.

Ports relocated to accommodate container infrastructure. New York's Manhattan piers were too small for cranes and yard space, so trade moved to Newark, repeating in London, Liverpool, and San Francisco.

asset_request.description: modern container port with large cranes and container stacks
asset_request.guidance: A clear image of a busy container port showing large cranes and organized container stacks, illustrating modern port infrastructure.

slot_panel.heading: Ports Relocate for Container Shipping
bullets: Manhattan piers too small for cranes

Since the large square and four triangles are unchanged, the leftover areas must be equal, proving c squared equals a squared plus b squared.

cases.title: What a half life really means

skeleton.brief: Explain what a half life really means, correcting a common misconception
Introduce carbon fourteen and its half life duration
Show how the quantity halves over successive half lives
Explain the decay curve never reaches zero, it halves forever

Emphasize that atoms do not age and decay probability is constant

narration.text: A half life is not how long something lasts. It is how long it takes for half of what is there to go.
Carbon fourteen is a radioactive isotope with a half life of about five thousand seven hundred and thirty years. This means it takes that long for half of a sample to decay.

slot_term.definition: A radioactive isotope of carbon used in dating ancient materials, with a half life of 5,730 years.
slot_term.caption: Also called radiocarbon
slot_term.heading: Carbon Fourteen

narration.text: Starting with one kilogram, after one half life you have half a kilogram left, after two half lives a quarter, and after three just an eighth.
The decay curve never reaches zero. It keeps halving forever, getting closer and closer but never quite disappearing.

slot_plot.heading: Radioactive Decay Curve
slot_plot.caption: Quantity halves continuously but never reaches zero

narration.text: The decay equation is N equals N nought times e to the minus lambda t, where lambda is the decay constant related to the half life.
A carbon fourteen atom does not age. Its chance to decay is the same whether it’s five thousand years old or freshly formed. There is no memory in it.

slot_quote.heading: "A carbon fourteen atom that has sat in a bone for five thousand years is exactly as likely to decay in the next second as one made this morning."

narration.text: This memoryless property is why radiocarbon dating works. The remaining proportion acts as a reliable clock, unaffected by the sample’s history.
